h1
In one ancient song, someone takes an axe to Zeus.
h2
His head splits open, and out leaps a goddess, already shouting.
h3
That goddess is Athena. Every poem and handbook we'll look at today agrees on that part. She came out of her father's head.
h4
What they can't agree on is who swung the axe. Or whether there was an axe at all.
h4b
And in one version, her mother is still inside him.
h5
So today we line up the suspects. We'll use the oldest poems that tell this story, a painted jar from Athens, and the Parthenon.
a1
Quick reminder. Last time, Zeus swallowed his first wife, Metis, when she was about to give birth to Athena.
a1b
Earth and Heaven had told him to. Metis was the wisest of gods and mortals, and her children were destined to be very wise.
a1c
First a daughter, equal to her father in strength and in wise understanding. After her, a son who would be king of gods and men.
a1d
So Zeus swallowed the mother, to make sure nobody would ever take his throne.
a2
Which leaves a puzzle. The daughter was already on her way. If her mother is inside Zeus, how does the baby get out?
a3
Hesiod's answer takes one line. Zeus himself gave birth to her, from his own head.
a3b
Then he gives her a string of titles. She's the queen, who delights in tumults and wars and battles.
a4
And that's it. He doesn't say how. He doesn't say if it hurt.
a5
He moves straight on to Hera, who is very angry and quarrelling with her husband.
a6
So Hera has a child of her own, without Zeus. That child is Hephaestus, the best craftsman among the gods.
a7
Keep him in mind. He's going to matter.
b1
Now, there's a longer version of this passage. It survives because another ancient writer quoted it, and scholars aren't sure Hesiod wrote it.
b1b
But it tells a very different story about Metis.
b2
Here, Zeus swallows her because he's afraid she'll bring forth something stronger than his thunderbolt.
b2b
And she gets pregnant after he swallows her. Inside him.
b3
Zeus gives birth by way of his head, on the banks of a river called Trito.
b4
And Metis never comes out. She stays hidden in his insides, wiser than gods and men.
b5
In there, the poem says, Athena gets the thing that will make her stronger than any other god. Then Zeus brings her out, already dressed for war.
b6
So the wisest being alive is sitting inside the king of the gods.
b7
And honestly, I think the main version points the same way. Hesiod says Zeus swallowed Metis so that the goddess might devise for him both good and evil.
c1
So where does the axe come from? Not from Hesiod.
c2
More than two hundred years later, around four hundred and sixty four B.C., a poet called Pindar wrote a victory song for Diagoras, a boxer from the island of Rhodes.
c3
Rhodes had its own story about the day Athena was born, and Pindar works it into the song.
c4
In his version, Athena was born by the handiwork of Hephaestus, under a bronze axe. She leapt from the crown of her father's head and cried aloud, and Heaven and Earth trembled at her.
c4b
At that moment, the sun god told his sons on Rhodes to build Athena an altar, and be the first to honor her.
c4c
But a cloud of forgetfulness came over them. They forgot to bring fire, so they made their offerings without a flame.
c4d
Zeus rained gold on the land anyway, and Athena made them the best craftsmen of all.
c4e
I'd call that a very flattering story to sing for a champion from Rhodes.
c5
And notice who gets the credit. Hephaestus, the smith. Our first suspect.
c6
Now go back to Hesiod for a second. If you read his poem in order, Athena is born first. Hephaestus comes after, out of Hera's anger.
c7
Read that way, the smith couldn't have held the axe. He wasn't born yet.
c7b
Unless you read the longer version. There, the quarrel with Hera and the birth of Hephaestus come first, and only then does Zeus swallow Metis.
c7c
Read in that order, the smith is already around.
c8
And Hephaestus isn't our only suspect.
c9
Centuries later, a handbook of Greek myths called the Library gives the job to Prometheus. Or, it adds, as others say, Hephaestus.
Two suspects, and the handbook won't pick one. It does name the place, though. The river Triton.
c10b
Almost the same name as the river in that longer Hesiod passage.
d1
So what did the birth look like? For that we have a short hymn to Athena, one of the Homeric Hymns. Those are old poems written in the style of Homer.
d1b
In the hymn, she comes out wearing warlike arms of flashing gold.
d2
Athena springs from the immortal head and stands before Zeus, shaking a sharp spear.
d3
Every god watching is struck with awe.
d4
Great Olympus reels at her strength. The earth around cries out, and the sea is tossed with dark waves.
d5
Even the sun stops. The sun god holds his horses still for a long while, until Athena takes the armor off her shoulders.
d6
And Zeus, the hymn says, is glad.
d7
There's no axe in this one at all. Nobody seems to be in any pain.
e1
That's the poetry. Now something you can actually go and see, and it's older than Pindar's song.
e2
This jar was painted in Athens in the sixth century B.C., more than two and a half thousand years ago. Today it's in the Louvre, in Paris.
e3
Find the top of Zeus's head. That small figure in a helmet, already armed, is Athena.
e4
The woman on the right is a mystery. One description says she's the goddess of childbirth, with a question mark. Another says Aphrodite.
e5
About a century later, Athens put the same moment somewhere much bigger.
e6
The Parthenon, the great temple of Athena on the Acropolis.
e6b
Centuries after it was built, the traveller Pausanias visited. He wrote that the sculptures over the entrance were all about the birth of Athena.
f1
So, who split Zeus's head open?
f2
Hesiod doesn't need anyone. Pindar says Hephaestus. The handbook says Prometheus, or maybe Hephaestus. And the hymn never mentions an axe.
f2b
If you want one name, the oldest poem here that names anybody is Pindar's. He names Hephaestus. Even though, if you read Hesiod's main version in order, the smith wasn't born yet.
f3
But if you ask me, the axe was never the point.
f4

Think about what Hesiod's poem gives us. Zeus swallows the wisest goddess there is, and keeps her inside him. And the daughter who comes out of his head is his equal, in strength and in wise understanding.
f5
That's my reading, not Hesiod's words. To me, this is a story about Zeus taking wisdom into himself. He swallows it, and it comes back out of his head, fully armed.
f6
Next time, our other suspect. Prometheus, the clever one who tricked Zeus, and the woman the gods made because of it.
